---
title: "Dimensionality Reduction and the Effect of Class Imbalance"
subtitle: "PCA, t-SNE and UMAP (2D and 3D) on the balanced, imbalanced and 3-class diabetes datasets"
output:
  pdf_document:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 3
    number_sections: true
    df_print: kable
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Compute the embeddings if the cache is missing (first run); otherwise reuse it.
if (!file.exists("dr_results/dr_embeddings.rds")) {
  source("dr_analysis.R")
}

cc  <- read.csv("dr_results/tables/class_counts.csv")
ov  <- read.csv("dr_results/tables/overlap_metrics.csv")
emb <- readRDS("dr_results/dr_embeddings.rds")

dsname <- c(balanced = "Balanced binary", imbalanced = "Imbalanced binary",
            threeclass = "3-class")
varexp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(emb), function(nm) {
  v <- emb[[nm]]$var_explained
  data.frame(Dataset = dsname[nm], PC1 = v[1], PC2 = v[2], PC3 = v[3],
             Cumulative = sum(v))
}))
```

This report visualises the three diabetes datasets in two and three dimensions
with **PCA**, **t-SNE** and **UMAP**, and uses the resulting geometry (together
with local-neighbourhood purity) to explain **why class imbalance causes the
models to collapse onto the majority class**, as observed in the earlier
logistic-regression / KNN / random-forest / classification-tree analysis.

# Data and preprocessing

- **Balanced binary**: 50/50 file (Diabetes\_binary), 67,136 rows.
- **Imbalanced binary**: derived from the 3-class file, 1 = prediabetes or
  diabetes (`Diabetes_012 > 0`), 236,378 rows.
- **3-class**: `Diabetes_012` = 0 (none), 1 (prediabetes), 2 (diabetes),
  236,378 rows.

All 21 health indicators were standardised (mean 0, sd 1). t-SNE and UMAP are
expensive on the full data, so a **stratified subsample of about 6,000 rows per
dataset** (class proportions preserved) was used for all projections, which
keeps the methods directly comparable. PCA is also shown on the same subsample.

```{r classcounts}
cc$share <- sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cc$share)
kable(cc, col.names = c("Dataset", "Class", "n", "Share"),
      caption = "Class sizes and proportions in each dataset.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
```

The class imbalance is dramatic: 50/50 in the balanced file, roughly 83/17 in the
imbalanced binary task, and 83/14/2.4 in the 3-class task, where **prediabetes is
only 2.4% of the data (about 1 in 35 compared with the majority class)**.

```{r varexp}
varexp[, 2:5] <- lapply(varexp[, 2:5], function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x))
kable(varexp, caption = "Variance explained by the first three principal components.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center")
```

The first three principal components capture only about **31%** of the total
variance in every dataset. The information that separates the classes is spread
across many dimensions, so any 2D/3D projection inevitably shows a lot of
overlap -- an early sign that the classes are not linearly separable in a
low-dimensional view.

# Balanced binary dataset

```{r, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("dr_results/figures/dr_2d_balanced.png")
```

```{r, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("dr_results/figures/dr_3d_balanced.png")
```

PCA shows partial separation along PC1 (no-diabetes tends to the left, diabetes
to the right), but the two clouds overlap heavily. t-SNE and UMAP reveal local
clusters, yet **within every cluster the two classes are intermingled**. Because
both classes are equally frequent, the locally mixed regions are split roughly
in half, and the models still predict both classes well (recall around
0.76--0.78). This is the "clean" reference case.

# Imbalanced binary dataset

```{r, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("dr_results/figures/dr_2d_imbalanced.png")
```

```{r, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("dr_results/figures/dr_3d_imbalanced.png")
```

The geometry is similar to the balanced case -- the minority (prediabetes or
diabetes) still overlaps the majority -- but now the majority completely
dominates the point cloud. Visually the minority points are a small fraction of
every dense region. This is the same overlap as before, now combined with a
strong prior in favour of the majority class.
